evidence.title: Fanatic
evidence.author: Ungemah, Joe
excerpts: From ultramarathon runners who push their bodies to the breaking point to the humble bottle collector who digs up old privies to find the perfect specimen, these individuals are amazing.
Far from traditional connotations of fanatics being strange or extreme, this book argues that fanaticism can bring us joy and interest to the world.
Through interviews and direct experience, this book captures stories of real-world fanatics who discovered something they were passionate about and made it core to their self-concept.
The types of fanaticisms profiled are wide-ranging, from the highly social to the esoteric, and sometimes directed at resolving regrets or coping with trauma.

A set of common motivations emerged, spanning the social, physical, cognitive, and emotive psychological domains, that when combined make a particular passion sticky and core to the fanatic’s identify.
To become a fanatic, individuals demonstrate both an openness to new experiences and commitment to stick with it.
For all the benefits that fanaticism provides, it can pose a risk to healthy living if it becomes all encompassing.

To help understand where that line is and what to do about it, interviews were held with experts in clinical and sport psychology, as well as others who use fanaticism proactively to build social connections and understanding.
With nearly an unlimited range of topics that could seed fanaticism, this book argues that we are all a fanatic about something or at least have the potential to become one.

evidence.title: Introduction
evidence.author: Ungemah, Joe
excerpts: Abstract This chapter introduces the concept of being a fanatic and the historical connotations that the term elicits.

Whereas common definitions of fanaticism emphasize strangeness or extreme behavior, the book is positioned to embrace fanaticism for all the benefits it provides while acknowledging that passion can sometimes go too deep and interfere with healthy living.

The introduction outlines the structure and content of the chapters with an overview of how personality and context come together to influence whether an individual will find a passion area and stick with it.

Positive and problematic versions of fanaticism are introduced, in addition to the social, physical, emotive, and cognitive psychological domains that provide the backbone to the book’s primary model.
A set of motivations are proposed, which are said to combine in unique patterns to drive and maintain fanatic behavior.
If harnessed, these motivations provide opportunities for human connection and the potential to heighten fanatic experiences.

evidence.title: Action
evidence.author: Ungemah, Joe
excerpts: Abstract The Conclusion ties together the wide range of fanatics profiled in this book by identifying a common set of motivations that propel individuals toward their specific passion area.

Whereas previous research has concentrated on evaluating the relative strength of an individual’s fanaticism, this book has unearthed the reasons why someone becomes a fanatic and is willing to invest time and energy in its pursuit.
A periodic table of twenty fanatic elements is proposed, which span the social, physical, cognitive, and emotive domains.
These elements come together into unique molecules that tell the story of what attracted a fanatic to a given passion area and kept them there.

Contributing to the molecule is a combination of the context, where the fanaticism is first encountered, and personality traits that predict whether an individual is likely to engage and stick with it.
Despite fanaticism’s potential to overtake healthy living, having a passion and sharing it with others brings happiness and meaning to the world.

evidence.title: Why Can't This Be Love
excerpts: "Why Can't This Be Love" is a song by the American rock band Van Halen for their seventh studio album, 5150 (1986).
The song was the group's first single with Sammy Hagar, replacing founding member David Lee Roth.
It was released on both 7" and 12"  formats with the latter having an extended version featuring extra lyrics.
In the US, it went to number three on the Billboard Hot 100 and hit number one on the Cashbox Top 100, the week of May 16.
It was a top 10 hit in the United Kingdom, Australia and Germany and a top 20 single in Canada, the Netherlands and Sweden.

evidence.title: Why Don't You Love Me (Hank Williams song)
excerpts: "Why Don't You Love Me" is a song by American singer and guitarist Hank Williams.
It was released as a single in 1950 with the B-side, "A House Without Love".

evidence.title: Why Can't We Live Together
excerpts: "Why Can't We Live Together" is a song written and recorded by Timmy Thomas in 1972.
A chart hit in the following year, it was included on the album Why Can't We Live Together and was one of the first major hits to feature a rhythm machine.

evidence.title: Why (Must We Fall in Love)
excerpts: "Why (Must We Fall in Love)" is a Diana Ross & the Supremes and The Temptations song released in 1970 as the second single from the album Together.

While the album's preceding single, "The Weight" was only released in the US and Canada, "Why (Must We Fall in Love)" was not released in North America, but was released as a single in the United Kingdom, peaking at 31 on the charts.
The UK single hit the charts in March 1970, three months after Ross had left the Supremes.
